newsitem.title: FRANCE: Carlos the Jackal frustrated in book damages bid.
newsitem.headline: Carlos the Jackal frustrated in book damages bid.

text.p: Self-styled "professional revolutionary" Carlos the Jackal on Wednesday lost a bid for 910,000 francs ($170,000) damages over a new book which the guerrilla mastermind says wrecks his chances of a fair trial.
In a procedural tussle, a Paris court dropped Carlos' appeal after his lawyer Frederic Pariente argued that he had not been given enough time to study objections from Seuil publishers.
The judge rebuked Pariente for describing his client as a "professional revolutionary" in his plea. He struck the case from the register after trying to have the attorney plead his cause.

Carlos, whose real name is Ilich Ramirez Sanchez, lost a similar emergency court action in October when he sought a ban on the book "Carlos: The Secret Networks of International Terrorism" by journalist Bernard Violet.
Pariente, who received the Seuil arguments at the weekend, told Reuters he planned to restart the procedure soon, virtually from scratch as only initial submissions will be retained.

In his plea, Pariente argues that the book treats Carlos as responsible for a string of bombings and assassinations in France, violating his right to be considered innocent until proven guilty by a court.
His legal complaint says the book illegally included confidential reports from the investigation, including French and former East German secret service documents.

"'Carlos' has always shown the greatest scorn for human life and for political and judicial institutions on which are based the democracies which he has always tried to destroy," wrote Seuil lawyer Dominique de Leusse in his submission.
"It is therefore at the least shocking that the person concerned -- once he has been jailed -- should resort to French legal provisions which protect human dignity," he said.

De Leusse argued that French rules governing the confidentiality of investigations did not apply to the author or to the publisher, and insisted that an interview Carlos reportedly gave the Paris-based Arab-language newspaper Al Watan Al Arabi in 1979 was genuine.
Carlos has since his arrest stated that the interview, in which he is quoted as taking responsibility for several attacks, was a fake planted by Arab secret services.
Spirited out of Sudan by French counter-espionage in 1994, Carlos is now awaiting trial in the Paris prison of La Sante.

He had been convicted in his absence by a French court and sentenced to life in prison for the 1975 killings of two secret service agents in Paris. He is also being investigated over a total of six bombings and killings in France.

Carlos's boldest attack was to lead the 1975 kidnapping of 11 OPEC oil ministers attending a conference in Vienna. France says he killed a total of 83 people in a series of attacks, mostly in Europe and the Middle East.
